lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn la nomenclatura \u:
"

In Stock nomenclature the cation is named first, then the anion. If the metal has more than one oxidation state (Fe, Cu, Pb, Sn…), it is written in Roman numerals in parentheses: FeCl₃ = iron(III) chloride; FeCl₂ = iron(II) chloride. For metals with a single state (Na, Ca, Al) it is not written.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa \u003cb\u003esiste:
"

The systematic one uses multiplicative prefixes: Fe₂O₃ = diiron trioxide; CaCl₂ = calcium dichloride. The traditional one uses suffixes for metals with two states: the lower ends in -ous and the higher in -ic (ferrous/ferric, cuprous/cupric). Today IUPAC recommends Stock and systematic; the traditional one is kept because of its use.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos halógenos forman:
"

Halogens form oxoanions with different numbers of O: hypochlorite (ClO⁻, +1), chlorite (ClO₂⁻, +3), chlorate (ClO₃⁻, +5) and perchlorate (ClO₄⁻, +7). The suffix -ite indicates fewer O and -ate more; hypo- and per- mark the extremes. The same pattern holds for nitrite/nitrate (+3/+5) and sulfite/sulfate (+4/+6). Move the control to go through the series.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUn \u003cb\u003eácido:
"

An acid is H⁺ + anion. If the anion ends in -ide, the acid is “hydro...ic acid” (HCl(aq): hydrochloric acid). If it ends in -ate, “...ic acid” (H₂SO₄: sulfuric acid); if it ends in -ite, “...ous acid” (H₂SO₃: sulfurous acid). A hydroxide is cation + OH⁻: Ca(OH)₂ calcium hydroxide.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUn compuesto iónico s:
"

An ionic compound is formed with cations (+) and anions (−) in the proportion that cancels the charge. It is found with the crisscross method: the charge of one ion becomes the subscript of the other (Al³⁺ and O²⁻ → Al₂O₃). Polyatomic ions take parentheses if their subscript is greater than 1: Ca(OH)₂, Al₂(SO₄)₃. Choose a cation and an anion and watch the assembly.

"
